title: Cap. VIII Resp.: propensity to mercy need not give special grace to most; praeterition is not desertion
pass_a_gloss: But God is more inclined from himself unto having mercy and doing good unto men, than unto deserting and destroying them. We grant it. But he who is most inclined unto having mercy and doing good is not wont to impart excellent and peculiar benefits either unto all or unto most. It suffices unto showing this propensity of God unto mercy, that he has mercy on all as to many effects of his mercy, although as to this special effect, of preparing special grace and of infallibly ordaining unto eternal life, he has mercy neither on all nor on most. Then to pass by or to reprobate is not the same as to desert and to destroy. Indeed all the reprobated or non-elect are at length deserted and destroyed: but that they were passed by or non-elect unto special grace proceeds from the mere will of God; but that afterward they were deserted and destroyed took origin from their intervening demerit. Thus far we have satisfied those arguments which Gregory of Valencia uses, on 1 of Aquinas, question 23, concerning Reprobation.
pass_b_english: But God is more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting and destroying men. We grant it. Yet the most merciful is not wont to impart excellent peculiar benefits to all or even to most. It is enough to show that propensity that he has mercy on all as to many effects of his mercy — even if, as to this special effect of preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life, he has mercy neither on all nor on most. Further: to pass by or reprobate is not the same as to desert and destroy. Yes, all the reprobate or non-elect are at length deserted and destroyed — but that they were passed by or non-elect as to special grace proceeds from God's mere will; that afterward they were deserted and destroyed took its origin from their intervening demerit. So far we have answered the arguments Gregory of Valencia uses on Aquinas I, q. 23, on Reprobation.
source_text: Sed Deus propensior est ex se ad miserendum et benefaciendum hominibus, quam ad eos deserendos et perdendos. Concedimus. At qui est propensissimus ad miserendum et benefaciendum, non solet eximia et peculiaria beneficia aut omnibus aut pluribus impertiri. Sufficit ad hanc propensionem Dei in misericordiam ostendendam, quod omnium misereatur quoad multa misericordiae suae effecta, quamvis quoad hoc speciale effectum, gratiam specialem praeparandi et ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter ordinandi, nec omnium nec plurium misereatur. Dein praeterire vel reprobare non est idem quod deserere et perdere. Deseruntur quidem et perduntur tandem omnes reprobati sive non-electi: sed quod praeteriti fuerint aut non-electi ad gratiam specialem, ex mera Dei voluntate prodit; quod autem postmodum deserti et perditi, ex interveniente illorum demerito originem sumpsit. Hactenus iis argumentis satisfecimus quibus utitur Gregorius de Valentia, in 1. Aquinat. qu. 23. de Reprobatione.
